lesson.title: Networks and the defenders who watch them
lesson.subtitle: Packets, routes, and layers of defence

video.title: Networks and the defenders who watch them
video.format_note: Animated explainer for students aged 12–16, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph — computer studies teacher (main character)
Dr Farah Rahman — university lecturer who visits schools to talk about security
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, speaking to the student)

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph holds up a phone with a photo; the photo breaks into tiles that fly off along different roads on a map.
scenes.animation: The photo shatters into tiles; tiles race along lines.
scenes.narration: When you send a photo to a friend, it doesn’t travel in one piece. It’s chopped into pieces that can race across the network by different roads. Today, let’s follow them, and meet the people who guard those roads.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the lesson title and the cyber track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark scales in with a small overshoot; title slides up.
scenes.on_screen_text: Networks and the defenders who watch them
scenes.narration: Today: how networks carry your messages, and how defenders keep them safe.

scenes.visual: A packet as an envelope with two address labels hops from a phone to a router, to another router, to a friend’s phone, where the tiles rejoin into the photo.
scenes.animation: The envelope hops node to node.
scenes.narration: Everything you send is split into small packets. Each packet carries two addresses, called IP addresses: where it’s from, and where it’s going. Routers pass it along, hop by hop, and your friend’s phone puts the pieces back together.

scenes.visual: A web of routers. One link is cut with scissors; packets curve around it on another path.
scenes.animation: The cut link flashes; packets reroute.
scenes.on_screen_text: Many roads, so one can break
scenes.narration: There are many roads between two places. If a cable is cut or a router fails, packets simply take another route. That’s why the internet keeps working when parts of it break.

scenes.visual: Three cards: a closed padlock, a document with a check seal, a signal tower with full bars.
scenes.animation: Cards appear as they are named.
scenes.narration: Defenders protect three things, and every attack hits at least one. Confidentiality: only the right people can read it. Integrity: nobody can change it unnoticed. Availability: it works when you need it.

scenes.visual: Dr Farah holds a printed mark sheet where one mark has been changed in red. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Dr Farah slides in; cards drop with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Someone secretly changes a student’s mark in the school’s records. Which goal did they break?

scenes.visual: The integrity card gets the check badge. The changed mark is caught by a fingerprint check and a log entry showing who changed it.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops; the log line highlights.
scenes.narration: Integrity. Nobody needed to read the mark or block the system: it was changed. Defenders protect integrity with fingerprints, signatures and records of who changed what.

scenes.visual: An old castle: an outer wall, a gate, guards, and a locked treasure room in the middle.
scenes.animation: The layers draw from the outside in.
scenes.narration: No single defence is enough, so defenders build layers, like an old castle. A wall, then a gate, then guards, then a locked room for the treasure. If one layer fails, the next still stands.

scenes.visual: A school network diagram: a firewall at the entrance, the office network fenced off from the students’ Wi-Fi, an update arrow, and a spare line to the internet.
scenes.animation: Each layer lights up as it is named.
scenes.narration: On a network, the layers look like this. A firewall decides which traffic may pass in and out. The school office network is kept apart from students’ Wi-Fi. Updates close known holes. And spare routes and backups keep things running when something fails.

scenes.visual: A security operations centre: analysts at screens with graphs; one alert flashes for a sign-in from far away at 3:00.
scenes.animation: The alert pulses; an analyst points at it.
scenes.narration: In banks, mobile money companies and hospitals, a team called a security operations centre watches the alarms day and night. They read logs: records of who connected, when and from where. Then they spot what doesn’t fit, like a sign-in from another country at three in the morning.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph holds up a phone showing an error page on results day; a queue of students waits. Three answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. On results day, the exam results website goes down for everyone. Which goal is hit?

scenes.visual: The availability card gets the check badge. Four summary cards line up.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right.
scenes.on_screen_text: Packets · Three goals · Layers · People watching
scenes.narration: Availability: nothing was read or changed, but nobody could use it. Remember: packets hop along many routes, defenders guard confidentiality, integrity and availability, and they build layers so one failure isn’t the end.

scenes.visual: A student at a desk draws the school’s network on paper, adding a firewall and a fence between the office and the students’ Wi-Fi.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: in the lab, break a few sensors and add relays until every message gets through. Then draw your school’s network on paper, and mark where each layer of defence would go.

checkpoints.prompt: Someone secretly changes a student’s mark in the school’s records. Which security goal did they break?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — integrity means data can’t be changed without anyone noticing.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — nobody had to read the mark or stop the system. The mark was changed, so integrity was broken.

checkpoints.prompt: On results day, the exam results website goes down for everyone. Which security goal is hit?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — nothing was read or changed, but nobody could use it when they needed it.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — nothing was read or changed. The site stopped working when people needed it: that’s availability.
